Authorities:
Under government eyes, the Pizzeria had managed to pass as a normal pizzeria. We know since the employees have contracts and the pizzeria has announcements for other enterprises.
Remote activated simulation C (R.A.S.C):

This is a machine created by Henry in FNAF 6 in which the general believes about it is that it works in a way that connects with a central server at all times so that it cannot cause duplication signatures. If this breaks, the sound of clients or children which the salvage animatronics will hear throughout the game is going to be shattered, letting them realise the illusion of activity. The R.A.S.C simulates the sounds to attract them and fake activity, this stopping them from escaping the labyrinth, evidenced by what Henry says here:
You don't even realize that you are trapped. Your lust of blood has driven you in endless circles.
Chasing the cries of children in some unseen chamber. Always seeming so near, yet somehow out of reach.
But, you will never find them, none of you will

This dialogue tells us how he kept them inside the labyrinth, trapping them inside it with the fake sounds to keep them there, pursuing something they can never actually reach. the R.A.S.C. blueprint also specifies that Variable Alpha must remain at 98.6°F. This internal heater setting mimics the exact core body temperature of a human, giving the illusion that there’s human inside the labyrinth as well. The heat uplink sync prevents the system from confusing its own false heat signature with a real person, or accidentally broadcasting multiple human signatures in the tracking software. Sensor Override

This feature allows a human operator, the player sitting at the office computer terminal, to manually hijack the automated tracking systems. By executing an override, you actively command the R.A.S.C. unit to move to a designated location, overriding its baseline idle programming.

So, basically, the R.A.S.C plays the background sound of the fake customers, but you can use the sensor override to hijack automated tracking systems and then make it mimic a sound of a person inside the labyrinth to lure them away to it.
Purpose of the salvaging time:

During Salvage time, we’re obligated to follow our contract, in which we have to follow the terms under paragraph 4, which are unknown. Now that we’ve gone over the basics of the salvage time, I’ll explain the audio prompts and their purpose. I’m assuming that the sounds played are a "test track" like you'd use on an old VHS player to see if it worked properly or an
audio alignment cassette

for an old tape deck. It's a series of sounds that should trigger unique reactions. For example, the animatronic might be programmed to respond to a scream, but there are different kinds of screams, a child in pain and a child in incredible joy, which discerning between the two is essential. Following this hypothetical, the high-pitched sounds, although nonsense to you and me, may be designed to test whether or not the animatronic can still perceive the difference between those two kinds of high noises. The layman's explanation is that this is a dog whistle for animatronics training. Any animatronic that responds properly to this is "functioning." One that does not is "broken." Now that I have given an explanation over what these functions do, and what the franchisee (Micheal) is likely given, it’s time for the importance of them within the scheme. Henry’s main goal here is just bringing these animatronics in, but he cannot make it seem suspicious for the worker he’d hired; which we’ll go over.

But Henry also gives you the choice to throw the salvaged animatronics out, diverting more suspicion from this other possibility alone within whoever the franchisee would be. Another diversion is that it can be seen in a way that Fazbear Entertainment is trying to save money and use animatronics from the past; so while it might seem strange, it’ll seem nothing too weird in the FNAF universe due to its alignment with past actions of Fazbear Entertainment. Then we can’t forget the audio prompts themselves. It’s for the reasons for what I’d already explained about the audio prompts, that being it’s a dog whistle to test their functionality. So this ends up having many reasons from the perspective of the franchisee, reducing all suspicions onto Henry true motives during the salvage time and long term during the whole work week. We also got the paperwork in the salvage sections of the game, the one you have to check off after each audio prompt, which are likely confirmation stuff for the franchisee (Micheal) to give to Henry so that he can know his plan is going accordingly while not putting himself at risk.

Obviously, what the worker is getting is different for what Henry is getting, that being if they’re responsive to the audio log, then he’d successfully gotten the right animatronics with the spirits. Due to how they’re programmed, outside informations such as springbonnie’s suit reacting to audio prompts, which is evident from FNAF 3; Molten Freddy and Scrap baby reasons to why the audio prompts simulate her is specific sound frequencies designed to trigger the hunting protocols of the remnant inside her. Lefty’s reasoning is because of a glitched aggression loop; the audio prompt causes an internal conflict between Lefty's automated programming and the restless soul inside her due to the "steady voltage" system to keep the Puppet subdued. This erratic data stream makes the animatronic glitch, move, and become highly hostile toward the worker. All of these specific reactions were taken into account for identification for Henry since he wasn’t the one salvaging, which is why if they’re responsive, they’re likely the right people Henry wants because of the knowledge I’d listed, meaning if they’re reactive to the audio, then they’re likely right animatronics, especially the specific audio such as the FNAF 1 music.

Now, Lefty here is a bit different, since if we don’t end up salvaging him, she’ll just end up in the rare finds auction, showing us that even if Lefty doesn’t get salvage, she’ll find herself in the Pizzeria anyways, which makes sense considering the fact that Henry designed it to capture his Daughter for the plan, so he would want it to be here. Franchisee tests & business fabrication:

Before getting into the main point, it’ll need to be made clear that the office gameplay section, tycoon sections both take place during daylight, the gameplay section in which you can hear audio of a crowd which is completely fake, meaning to subconsciously effect the franchisee mind that it’s real, although the blockage of the business operating is something not exactly realised.

Now, in FNAF 6, if you increase the liability risk level through purchasing risky, low-quality, or marked-down catalog items; you get hit by lawsuits at the end of day. Why? Well, a lot of people assume that these are real, but i obviously don’t, because the lawsuits are completely fabricated by Henry. Why? Well, I personally think that Henry is testing the franchisee (Micheal) reliability, it being a stimulate penalty generated by Henry’s management software to test if Michael will take responsibility, pay the fine, or let the business sink. Michael fails the test by incurring too many penalties, Henry uses "bankruptcy" as a formal excuse to terminate his contract and scrub his employment record, wiping his hands of an unreliable partner before the main trap is sprung.

But that’s only one of the routes in which Henry carefully monitors reliability in his franchisee. We also got the blacklisted ending, in which if you’re too reckless (getting over 50 Liability Risk level or higher without going bankrupt) Henry will blacklist you, wiping the security footage clean and erasing all traces of our employment from Fazbear Entertainment Files. Outside from this, if you also don’t follow the special obligation from Paragraph 4, Micheal’s employment will be terminated. What all of these are testing is the franchisee reliable as a function operator in Henry’s scheme, and if he’s not fitted, these three endings will be the cause. Obviously, this is also apart of the concealment factor of the scheme, maintaining the image that this is a “real” business; even getting actual sponsors (Fiztime Popsoda - $250 Marty's Plungers - $500 Flo's Glossy Floss - $1000 Wacky Wart Paste - $2500 Lally's Lollies - $5000) for this to further ground the business in reality, while they’re actually just misleading factors.

The concealment aspect of this plan, if you ask me, is just wonderful, so I wanna go more in-depth in this. Aspects such as how the business functions are seemingly set up for the franchisee to not see through, such as the salvaging conditions, the work they’re obligated to do in the tycoon section of the game, or the little things such as the advertisements you get on the screen during the gameplay section are all clever, and targets you almost subconsciously due to mundane they actually are.  The reasoning behind it is because I think what Henry targets here is a very specific (although not clear in what I’m saying) part of the psychology which is that the information reaches subconscious acceptance due to the cleanliness of the fabricated information. These are not things that were consciously taken note off, and checking it off as valid, these were things already checked off unforced by conscious thought.

Take Micheal for E.G: he Isn’t questioning why and checking consciously for the fabricated information, it’s just something naturally done without him actually thinking about it. It’ll be like:  “Oh lawsuits, damn” rather than “why did I get a lawsuit?” While for William it’ll be: “what is Henry up too” rather than “is this business fake?” Although the animatronics are more limited in their information because of the fact that they’re only hearing the noise of a busy business rather than seeing; while lefty… uhh, well she’s confusing here, but it’s entirely possible that she just sneaks in or Henry plays those sounds when she’s gone from the main area of the location.  The Lawsuits in this are a noticeable weak point, although not a very strong one. You can win the lawsuits (although the percentage is 16 - 20%) so the win rate isn’t high, but if you do win, well I guess Henry is just going to pay it to keep it up, especially since he’s not gonna care if he’s result in this all is death. Now obviously Micheal is not seeing what’s  happening,  because he’s fighting for his life in the labyrinth; while the lawsuits require proof that the events actually happened, so the person who files the suit must present facts, documents, or witness statements to show the court that the event took place and caused harm. Without any evidence, the judge or jury will dismiss the case. With this into consideration, the lawsuits that Micheal have can’t exactly be questioned about, because of the burden of proof needed for the lawsuit to even take motion in the first place.

Proof for the lawsuits being fake? Well, the content inside of them are just ridiculous. Stuff such as breaking 106 bones, some boy being hospitalised for 10 months, another girl being in a coma for 10 weeks, and another bite happening are all ridiculous. Like seriously? Another Bite? I’ll make you proud, daddy
” which is why she’ll refer to this as a gift a lot in her dialogue in FNAF 6.

Especially Henry, who through the dynamic were presented with the other media, is written with jealousy, admiration, and much more. Now, moving on from this, Afton also said he couldn’t resist a promise like this, which is in reference towards the said trap, which speaks to us that he’s admitting that he couldn’t help himself but just walk into this trap of Henry and dismantle it, proving himself better; his arrogance making him believe he’s not in any sort of true danger. This is likely rooted in the fact that he survived both of his near death experience of the springlock failure, and burning fire of the horror attraction in FNAF 3; making him believe he had some sort of invincibility to the point that he can just survive this one. He always comes back. Henry would figure this out because it’s very likely he started to put in motion this scheme after learning the news of the fire in FNAF 3.

But outside of Henry abusement towards William’s pride, I think that fact that William wants to figure out this trap he doesn’t fully know, only aware about, makes him fascinated in the others, which is evident by his dialogue here: “
fascinating… what they have become

”  which says to us the obvious, that being he’s fascinated. Why though? What is this so fascinating to him, the others in the same labyrinth as him? Well, I think it’s two reasons for it: Afton’s need to figure out this deceptive calling, and just the overall nature of how they became to be. Take Elizabeth as one of the example. She’s showcasing a praise towards her father, when before, she seemed a bit more resentful towards him; then take Molten Freddy, who was the Funtime animatronics, now this almost unrecognisable figure of his making. He’ll stay because of many things, and these are just showcasings of multiple stuff. Elizabeth thinking that it’s him behind this, and Molten Freddy outcome from what he remembered.

It’ll get to the point for Afton that he’ll just come into the trap either way even if he’s not salvage (something you’ll need to do with the rest of them) which is very important, because it just demonstrates such a robust depth of this trap Henry had laid out for William that he basically controlling his desires. But, to make it clear, this doesn’t give other characters outside of FNAF a strong point of advantage over Afton, since I believe this trap had strong exploitation in it because Henry was the one doing it, which Henry was very much aware about. You’ll need a very specific established dynamic which Henry had with William for you to really achieve this trap succession, or else William will just look at it, get irritated that someone think they can outsmart him, and probably not walk into it.

Now, people will go out of their way to say that Henry was business partners with William! He knew him for many years and they’re likely close, so it’s immediately downgraded because of the length of Henry knowing Afton. This is a valid process, and I would let it be if it
were

true, but I believe got a refute for this claim. I believe that Henry was blindsided of the side which was later exploited in FNAF 6, because I think Afton had a more public persona which he demonstrated. Where I can show a demonstration of this is with the interview at the very start of Sister Location, which he was being interviewed by board members. In this, Afton showcased a more professional, cooperative, but smug attitude, one that you would expect from a business man like Afton was. PJ (William’s voice actor) said that Scott wanted Afton to sound like snake-oil salesman, summarising it as the “clam sociopath” in the interview; one that PJ said was remained by Hannibal Lecter, the one from the silence of the lamb movie. Particularly that calm demeanour, which Afton had in this interview with the board members.

Obviously, Afton, from what we’d been shown is usually a lot more erratic, expressive, and performative compared to this one interview. I bring this up because I find it very important for Afton public persona, which would had been that more calm one which he demonstrated towards the board members (being one of the times which Afton talked publicly like this) compared to the rest of his attitude, which are usually a lot more closeted from public view; that sadistic man. Point being, Henry more than likely presented this side of Afton a lot more than his true self, since as we know, it’s public… I know. Henry constructed a situation where William’s recognition of the deception actually failed to prevent his participation because Henry understood the psychological incentives that would override William’s caution
